record_reviews.summary: Sulivan's incomplete 2 February letter answers Darwin's dispersal questions in four surviving paragraphs: Falkland shore vegetation consisted of mainland-drifted birch trees used as ship fuel; he cannot recall whether Beagle's paint was spoiled by seeds or dust; Falkland snipe leave in winter; and he recalls a woodcock striking the return merchant ship in August, over 500 miles from land. The final recollection is a specific long-distance bird record, but its question-bearing Darwin letter is absent.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 2 February [1855] is a single XML day; the body is an incomplete incoming letter (†) and does not itself date when Darwin read or used the observation.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Surviving prose is attributed to Sulivan, B. J. writing to Darwin; direction is to_darwin. Editorial annotations and footnotes were read separately and are not merged into the body.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Darwin response to this incoming Sulivan fragment is among the packet targets; the specific bird observation remains a possible knowledge input only, with its incoming prompt unresolved.

record_reviews.summary: Long Sulivan letter from the Falklands first reports military conditions, then answers Darwin's questions about cattle limb/horn proportions, colour variation by locality and breeding season. It continues through horses, geology, coal, pebbles, fossils and specimens, with several postscripts and an explicitly incomplete/additional-page structure. The two preserved diagrams show a cliff slope/dip profile and a section of sandstone, pebble bed, peat and sea level; they were viewed directly and are not treated as prose evidence.

record_reviews.summary: Sulivan reports that he must remain abroad another year, explains why fossils may not safely travel in casks, recounts seeing Rugendas, and asks for Darwin's response to his earlier Falklands letter because he wants to know whether the fossils surprised him. This establishes an unanswered request for a reply, not a prompt for the 1855 bird observations.

Two available diagrams were visually inspected: one labels slope, dip, sea-level and a deep valley; the other diagrams sandstone, pebble bed, peat, early soil and a stream course. They belong to 1843 context and are not evidence of 1551.

Later Darwin mentions of Sulivan or Falklands material were searched in the preserved collection; they show ongoing use of earlier Sulivan material but do not identify a surviving Darwin response to 1551. No later forwarding event was counted as a new edge.
